..
As of 400 PM Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Waves of showers and storms with a risk for 
excessive rainfall and flooding will focus along a slow-moving, 
outflow-reinforced/strengthened cold front that passes through 
central NC from now through Thursday night.

Scattered thunderstorms will begin to move into the NW Piedmont over 
the next few hours. These cells will then develop into a broken 
convective line pushing eastward through the Triangle during the 
evening and overnight hours, maintaining the threat for isolated to 
scattered strong to severe storms. It is fairly cool and stable near 
the VA border with temperatures only in the upper-70s, so it may be 
difficult to get much of a damaging wind threat there. Across the NW 
Piedmont, on the other hand, temperatures are still in the upper-80s 
with SBCAPE around 1500-2000 J/kg. If storms can outrun the boundary 
into the warm sector, this is likely where the greatest severe 
threat will be. However, while 0-1 km shear is not impressive (10-15 
kts), still can't rule out a quick spinup with any convection, even 
on the cool side of the boundary. Localized excessive rainfall and 
flash flooding will be the bigger threat, particularly in urban 
areas.

By late tonight and Thursday morning, the activity is expected to 
spread south and east into the Sandhills and Coastal Plain as well. 
While the severe threat will generally subside tonight with loss of 
instability, storm motion running parallel to the stalling boundary 
will cause repeating waves of heavy rain to train over the same 
areas, shifting the primary hazard to more widespread flash 
flooding. Thus a Flood Watch is in effect for all of central NC, 
beginning across the northern half this afternoon and evening, then 
across our southern half overnight tonight. The WPC Excessive 
Rainfall Outlook for today/tonight highlights a Moderate Risk (Level 
3/4) clipping the northeastern Coastal Plain (near Roanoke Rapids) 
with a Slight Risk (Level 2/4) across roughly the northern half. 
Urban areas, small streams, and creeks will be particularly 
vulnerable to rapid runoff and localized flash flooding. Mainstem 
rivers will also begin to rise in response to heavy rainfall, though 
they are expected to remain below minor flood stage through at least 
Thursday morning.

The cold front will move only slightly south and east on Thursday, 
and with rich Gulf moisture from Tropical Storm Bertha continuing to 
funnel NE along the front, another day of heavy rainfall and 
possible flash flooding is expected, this time across all of central 
NC. WPC QPF on Thursday and Thursday night is 1-2 inches on average 
across the region, except across our far north as the front sags 
south of there. As always, locally higher amounts will be possible, 
with 12z HREF LPMM depicting potential for 2-4 inches to the south 
and east of Raleigh. The 12z HREF and REFS depict neighborhood 
probabilities of exceeding 6-hour FFG peaking across our area from 
12-18z Thursday. Thus there is a moderate (level 3 of 4) risk for 
excessive rainfall across eastern NC that includes much of our 
Coastal Plain, with a slight (level 2 of 4) risk for the rest of 
central NC outside of the far NW. No mainstem rivers are forecast to 
reach minor flood stage at this time, but it can't be ruled out if 
excessive rain falls directly over a basin. Still, urban and small 
stream flash flooding will be the biggest and most widespread threat.

One silver lining is the severe threat at least looks to decrease on 
Thursday. This is due to the Eastern US troughing beginning to 
flatten, resulting in a weakening of the mid-level flow, and the 
best instability shifting to our southern zones where shear will be 
less. However, a few strong storms with water-loaded downbursts or a 
quick spinup still can't be totally ruled out, mainly in the south.


KEY MESSAGE 2... The slow moving cold front across the Carolinas 
will settle south and stall across the southern Carolinas for Friday 
and into the weekend with the area of widespread rain shifting south 
and the rainfall intensity decreasing on Friday and especially 
Saturday.

While there will still be a threat for heavy rainfall on Friday, it 
looks to be less overall compared to today and Thursday and shifts 
to mainly south and east of Raleigh, as the cold front shifts south 
and stalls from SC to the southern NC coast. WPC QPF from Friday 
into Saturday has decreased compared to yesterday, with just 0.25-
0.5 inches expected on average for most of the area, except 0.5-1.5 
inch totals across the southern Piedmont, Sandhills, and 
central/southern Coastal Plain. A shortwave trough moving through 
the TN Valley and southern Appalachians may actually enhance the 
moist air mass again on Saturday as PW values increase to 2-2.5 
inches, along with providing additional forcing for ascent. However, 
we will still be on the cool side of the boundary, which should keep 
rainfall rates lower than they had been.
